tldr: This paper proposes a foundation model for robots that natively integrates a "Thinker" for multimodal understanding, a "Talker" for streaming speech generation, and an "Actor" that directly generates body motions and facial expressions. The system achieves pointing at visually perceived objects in a scene alongside gestures that naturally synchronize with speech timing at low latency.
hero_caption: An example interaction applying XBot-Omni to real humanoid robots (PrimeBOT Q1 and AGIBOT X2). In step with the speech progression, shy facial expressions and gestures (①), directional indication motions (②), and accurate pointing motions toward a visually detected apple (③) are executed with multimodal, high-temporal-precision synchronization.
overview:
Recent omni foundation models (Omni-LLMs) can seamlessly understand and generate text, images, and speech, but they cannot directly produce physical expressions such as gestures and facial expressions needed by embodied agents like robots interacting with humans. Conventional conversational robot systems mainly rely on a pipeline that passes generated audio waveforms to an external gesture generation module (Audio-to-Gesture). However, this often loses context and intent regarding which object in the visual scene to point at, and it introduces latency while waiting for the audio waveform.

To tackle this, the study introduces XBot-Omni, featuring a "Thinker–Talker–Actor" architecture that unifies thinking, speaking, and acting within a single framework. The dedicated Actor directly generates real-time body motions and facial expressions by extracting context and referent semantics from the internal representations of the Thinker (which handles multimodal reasoning) and tracking speech progress from the internal states of the Talker (which handles streaming speech generation). Because it references native states directly without waiting for waveform decoding, motion can begin with a latency of just 527 milliseconds.

Across 7 comprehensive benchmarks, the Thinker achieved top-tier performance on multimodal video understanding (86.30% on Daily-Omni) and spatial reasoning. Furthermore, the Actor scored 1.383 on context-aware semantic gesture quality, significantly outperforming existing methods (0.608), while demonstrating that pointing at visual 3D object positions can be realized with high spatial accuracy and precise timing.
contributions: Proposed XBot-Omni, an integrated architecture extending omni foundation models to embodied physical expression by coupling a Thinker, Talker, and Actor via native internal representations.
Achieved low-latency (527 ms) and highly accurate speech-motion synchronization by streaming motions and facial expressions directly from Talker internal states, bypassing audio waveform re-encoding.
Established Spatial Grounding and Pointing Training (SGPT), which identifies 3D coordinates of objects in the visual scene and adapts physical motions to match referring expressions during speech.
Constructed an advanced multimodal training pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning (GRPO), and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD).

sections.heading: Giving Omni-Models a Body: Enter Thinker–Talker–Actor
sections.summary: In human interaction, nonverbal behaviors such as gestures and facial expressions are closely tied to speech content, visual scenes, and timing. This paper proposes XBot-Omni, introducing an Actor component that generates motions and facial expressions directly from the native representations of an omni-model.
sections.details:
In embodied interaction where humans and robots converse within physical environments, the timing and context of nonverbal behaviors are crucial. For example, pointing in the wrong direction while saying "that apple over there" or desynchronizing words and body language obscures the intended message.

Existing omni-models integrate text, images, and audio to speak, but lack the capability to directly generate robot motions. Traditional conversational systems typically feed model-generated audio waveforms into a separate Audio-to-Gesture (A2G) generator. This design suffers from two major flaws: relying solely on audio waveforms discards visual context about which object in the scene the robot intends to point at, and re-extracting acoustic features after waveform synthesis incurs substantial response latency.

XBot-Omni addresses these challenges through a unified Thinker–Talker–Actor architecture. The Thinker interprets multimodal inputs to build response intentions, the Talker synthesizes streaming speech, and the Actor directly receives internal (native) representations from both to generate physical movements and facial expressions.

The Actor incorporates three internal mechanisms: a Motion Generator that produces low-latency actions directly from Talker internal states without waiting for waveforms, a Semantic Action Controller that extracts concrete gesture specifications from speech intent and visual context, and a Speech–Action Aligner that synchronizes speech progression with action execution timing. This enables contextually and temporally synchronized physical behavior at low latency without waveform decoding overhead.

sections.heading: Three Minds in Sync: The Thinker–Talker–Actor Architecture
sections.summary: XBot-Omni consists of three elements: the Thinker for contextual reasoning, the Talker for streaming speech generation, and the Actor for body motions and facial expressions. The Actor drives real-time motion by directly receiving internal latent representations from the Thinker and Talker rather than an external audio waveform.
sections.details:
The overall architecture balances specialized roles with tight information sharing.

### 2.1 Overview
The system receives text, images, audio, video, and dialogue history as input. The Thinker interprets the situation and constructs a response, the Talker converts it into streaming speech, and the Actor simultaneously produces corresponding body motions and facial expressions. Although the generation process for each modality is modular, sharing the Thinker's contextual representations and the Talker's speech progress states with the Actor enables a fully aligned multimodal response.

### 2.2 Thinker: Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning
Text passes through a tokenizer, while image and video frames are converted into visual representations via a dedicated vision encoder. Audio is transformed into mel-spectrograms and projected into the backbone space through an Audio Transformer (AuT). In addition, video and audio patches are annotated with second-level text timestamps beforehand, allowing the model to explicitly perceive temporal ordering and absolute timing.

### 2.3 Talker: Streaming Speech Generation
The Talker generates speech autoregressively. Built on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) backbone, it uses multi-token prediction (MTP) to sequentially predict speech tokens, which a codec decoder converts into an acoustic waveform. Crucially, the Talker exposes its intermediate internal hidden states to the Actor in real time. This directly connects speech features to motion generation without intermediate waveform decoding or audio re-encoding.

### 2.4 Actor: Embodied Response Generation
The Actor contains two generation branches: body motion and facial expression. In the body motion branch, gesture requirements (semantics and 3D pointing coordinates) are extracted from Thinker representations, and discrete motion tokens are generated autoregressively in sync with Talker progress before being decoded into continuous trajectories. In the facial expression branch, continuous changes are synthesized using a generator based on a Chunk Transformer and flow matching (a diffusion-like method capable of fast, high-quality continuous generation).

captions.F2: Overall view of the XBot-Omni Thinker–Talker–Actor architecture. Shared latent representations extracted by the Thinker are fed into the Actor's motion and expression control, while real-time hidden states from the Talker's autoregressive speech generation are supplied directly to motion and expression generation processes via the Speech–Action Aligner.

sections.heading: Aligning Words and Body: Nonverbal Behavior from Native Representations
sections.summary: This section details how the Actor leverages Thinker and Talker internal states to create movements and facial expressions synchronized with intent and speech. Coordinating the Motion Generator, Semantic Action Controller, and Speech–Action Aligner smoothly blends visual pointing with meaningful gestures.
sections.details:
Here is how the Actor aligns physical expressions with semantic meaning and speech timing.

### 3.1 Motion Generator
The Motion Generator receives the Thinker state sequence $H^{\mathrm{th}}$ and Talker state sequence $H^{\mathrm{sp}}$. A causal adapter projects the Talker states into a motion conditioning feature space $e$. At motion step $t$, the generator autoregressively predicts discrete motion tokens $z_t$ conditioned on adapted speech history $e_{\leq t}$, active semantic event conditions $U_t$, and prior generated motion history. When performing pointing gestures, the generated trajectory and 3D target coordinates are passed to a kinematics adapter, directing the arm toward the target via inverse kinematics (IK) in the robot's frame of reference.

### 3.2 Semantic Action Controller
This module defines semantic and spatial parameters for gestures based on speech content. It extracts the gesture category $y_e$ (e.g., pointing, waving), semantic parameters $a_e$ (such as arm choice and 3D target position), and the corresponding text span from Thinker states. For visual pointing, visual grounding and depth estimation identify the 3D target position, which is transformed into the robot's body-centric coordinate system. These event representations modulate intermediate layers of the motion generation network via feature-wise scale and shift coefficients (Equations 2 and 3). A completion head also predicts whether an action has reached its expressive core or is ready for transition (release).

### 3.3 Speech–Action Aligner
This component governs when gestures should start. It constructs query vectors $q_n$ from Talker hidden states and keys $k_i$ from Thinker text positions, estimating current speech progress $\widehat{p}_n$ with a forward transition probability model (Equation 4). By predicting when the event-associated text position (anchor $i_e$) will be spoken and subtracting the lead preparation time $d_{y_e}$, it computes the action start time $T_{e}^{\mathrm{start}}$ (Equation 5). This enables precise synchronization, ensuring the hand points toward the target at the exact moment words like "on the right" are spoken.

### 3.4 Facial Expression Generation
In the facial expression branch, a Chunk Transformer summarizes Thinker semantics and Talker speech features into a temporal conditioning vector $C_j$. Conditioned on this vector, a Conditional Flow Matching generator synthesizes a continuous facial expression sequence $\widehat{F}_j$ from Gaussian noise (Equation 6), which plays back synchronously on the shared timeline alongside body motions.

sections.heading: From Thought to Physical Expression: A Three-Stage Training Strategy
sections.summary: Large-scale multimodal dialogue and motion data are curated via an agentic pipeline to train the Thinker and Actor in stages. The Thinker is trained using SFT, RL, and multi-teacher distillation, while the Actor progresses from speech adaptation to semantic control and vision-based pointing.
sections.details:
To achieve natural interaction and physical movement, the training data and learning procedures are carefully structured.

### 4.1 Large-Scale, High-Quality Embodied Dialogue Data
Existing datasets focus heavily on short video clips or pure manipulation tasks, lacking natural interaction dynamics and real-time responsive behaviors. In response, this study combined public datasets with custom-collected human-human and human-robot dialogue data featuring synchronized audio, gestures, facial expressions, and visual feeds. In addition, an agentic auto-annotation pipeline orchestrating ASR, object tracking, and action recognition tools was developed to generate temporally consistent instruction-following and QA data at scale.

### 4.2 Thinker Training
Post-training of the Thinker is divided into three stages:
- **Stage 1: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)**: Imparts broad capabilities in first-person dialogue context comprehension, speaker identification, and turn-taking timing.
- **Stage 2: Reinforcement Learning (RL) with Specialized Experts**: Uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) combining rule-based rewards (objective correctness) and model-based rewards (LLM-as-a-judge) to train specialized expert policies for distinct task domains.
- **Stage 3: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD)**: Merges expert capabilities into a single Thinker model by having domain experts guide the student model on its self-generated response trajectories via token-level reverse KL divergence minimization (Equation 7).

### 4.3 Actor Training
The Actor is trained progressively across three stages:
- **Stage 1: Native State Adaptation and Speech Alignment**: Trains a causal adapter to predict acoustic features from frozen Talker hidden states using normalized feature regression (Equation 8), while optimizing aligner position prediction loss (Equation 9).
- **Stage 2: Semantic Event Motion Training**: Learns semantically grounded motion sequences using weighted cross-entropy loss on motion tokens (Equation 10) and a balanced loss for action completion prediction (Equation 11).
- **Stage 3: Autoregressive Rollout and Synthesis Training**: Trains the model with its own past predicted motion histories (including prediction errors) as inputs to prevent compounding errors and ensure smooth transitions. The facial expression branch is trained concurrently using a flow matching loss (Equation 13).

### 4.4 Perception-to-Action Training (SGPT) and Real-World Integration
To achieve pointing at visually detected objects, Spatial Grounding and Pointing Training (SGPT) is introduced. Object detection and depth estimation locate 3D positions in camera coordinates, which are converted to the robot's body-centric frame (Equation 14) and passed to the Actor. Fine-tuning the Actor on a mixture of referring demonstration data and regular conversational motion data (Equation 15) allows visual pointing gestures to blend into dialogue while keeping the Thinker and Talker frozen.

sections.heading: From Multimodal Understanding to Motion Quality: Verified on 7 Benchmarks
sections.summary: The Thinker's reasoning capabilities, the Actor's motion quality and speech synchronization, and visual pointing precision were evaluated across 7 benchmarks. XBot-Omni achieved top accuracy on comprehensive video dialogue benchmarks and significantly outperformed prior methods on semantic gesture quality and 3D pointing accuracy.
sections.details:
To assess system capabilities from multiple angles, experiments were conducted across 7 benchmarks spanning 4 categories.

### 5.1 Thinker Evaluation (Multimodal & Spatial Understanding)
- **Daily-Omni (Everyday Audio-Visual Understanding)**: XBot-Omni achieved an overall accuracy of 86.30%, surpassing strong baselines such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus (84.74%) and Gemini-3.1-Pro. Substantial improvements emerged in audio-visual alignment (+2.97 points) and event order reasoning (+2.65 points).
- **ReTurn (5-Turn Context-Updating Dialogue)**: With an overall accuracy of 84.00%, it outperformed the baseline (70.04%) by 13.96 points, showing a notable +37.60 point leap on the "Reground" task involving context corrections.
- **EgoProx & ERIBench (Egocentric Spatial & Intent Reasoning)**: It outperformed prior models by over 25 points on object proximity estimation and posted top scores on ERIBench for spatial relations (59.17% vs 38.18%) and visual grounding (69.81%).

### 5.2 Motion Quality and Speech Synchronization
Evaluations on the BEAT2 test set and a custom test set covering 10 semantic targets compared the model against recent methods like EMAGE and Semantic Gesticulator.
- **Fréchet Gesture Distance (FGD)**: Measuring distributional divergence from human motion, XBot-Omni achieved 1.351, closest to natural human movement among all compared methods (1.389 to 9.817).
- **Semantic Quality (SQ, 0–3 Scale)**: In blind evaluations using Gemini 3.8 Flash, XBot-Omni reached an overall average of 1.383, more than doubling the best baseline of 0.608. It showed wide leads in directional gestures (1.750 vs 0.313) and spatial size depictions (1.000 vs 0.500).
- **Co-speech Timing (CT)**: The percentage of distinct gestures executed at appropriate speech timings reached 85.19% (46/54 cases), generating synchronized gestures more accurately and frequently than baselines (40.00% to 70.59%).

### 5.3 Visually Grounded Action (Pointing Precision)
- **Spatial Perception**: On TraceSpatial-Bench, 3D localization success reached 67.00% for start points and 68.00% for end points, exceeding baselines by over 20 points.
- **Pointing Evaluation**: Introducing SGPT boosted spatial accuracy from 0.357 to 0.990 and temporal alignment from 0.654 to 0.851, approaching human reference levels (spatial 0.999, temporal 0.985).
- **System Latency**: The median first-motion latency from the start of interaction to the output of physical movement was 527 milliseconds, demonstrating practical responsiveness for streaming conversational settings.

sections.heading: How Does This Differ from Prior Work? Bridging Omni-LLMs and Motion Generation
sections.summary: Recent Omni-LLM studies focus on streaming audio, video, and language, but do not generate physical motions. Meanwhile, motion generation struggles to directly incorporate visual scene intent. Natively linking these two domains sets XBot-Omni apart.
sections.details:
To understand XBot-Omni's position, we examine its relation to two primary research avenues.

### The Rise of Omni-LLMs
Models integrating text, audio, and vision have evolved from early discrete-token frameworks like NExT-GPT and AnyGPT to low-latency streaming speech models such as Mini-Omni2, Baichuan-Omni, and Qwen2.5/3-Omni. However, these models remain confined to perception and speech/text generation, lacking mechanisms to natively output physical actions grounded in a physical environment. XBot-Omni differs fundamentally by introducing the Actor as a third core pillar.

### Embodied Interaction and Visually Grounded Motion Generation
In co-speech motion generation, frameworks such as EMAGE, Semantic Gesticulator, and RoboGesture have advanced considerably. Works like MIBURI and Motion-Omni have also explored streaming and integration with speech-language models. Yet, no prior work unified omni-model reasoning with visually grounded pointing—interpreting visual scenes during dialogue (such as "that red apple on the table") and orienting physical actions toward those objects. XBot-Omni represents the first omni-model that directly couples visual scene understanding with gesture generation.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Toward Robots that Converse with the World Through Words and Body
sections.summary: XBot-Omni extends the omni foundation model paradigm to robotic embodiment by integrating thinking, speaking, and acting via native representations. Unifying visual and auditory understanding with real-time generation of physical movement and facial expressions provides a foundation for intelligent robots interacting in the physical world.
sections.details:
This work proposed XBot-Omni, extending the omnimodal paradigm to robot-specific modalities: body motions and facial expressions.

The collaborative Thinker–Talker–Actor architecture connects multimodal contextual reasoning, speech output, and real-time generation of semantically and temporally aligned nonverbal behaviors end-to-end. Through an agentic data generation pipeline, reinforcement learning with multi-teacher distillation, and staged Actor training incorporating spatial grounding, the robot can identify objects in visual scenes, articulate appropriate verbal responses, and smoothly point toward targets.

XBot-Omni establishes an extensible milestone toward general-purpose robot agents capable of living and interacting naturally alongside humans in the physical world.

takeaways: Generating gestures directly from Talker internal states without waiting for audio waveforms enables speech-motion synchronization at a low latency of 527 ms.
Embedding 3D spatial coordinates from visual scenes into gesture control vectors directly translates omni-model reasoning into physical pointing actions.
In Thinker training, creating task-specific RL experts and consolidating them via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) proves highly effective for context updating and spatial reasoning.
limitations: Motion quality evaluation relies primarily on automated assessments (Gemini scoring) over controlled, short responses; subjective human evaluation and large-scale real-robot trials in extended, open-ended dialogues remain insufficient.

While spatial pointing accuracy reaches near-human levels, motion smoothness metrics (such as FGD and beat alignment) exhibit slight drops compared to base models, leaving a trade-off between spatial precision and naturalness.

On certain tasks, such as Intent Inference in ERIBench, the model scores below the strongest baselines, showing that enhanced spatial reasoning does not uniformly transfer across all reasoning capabilities.
